subtopic: DOMESTICATION OF MUSK-OX
DOMESTICATION OF MUSK-OX
speechtext:
1.	For how long, and In what locations, have experiments been going on into the domestication of the musk-ox?
2.	At each of the locations where such experiments are being conducted (a) how many head of stock are there (b) how many births have occurred each year since the experiments began?
3.	How much have these experiments cost so far (a) in Canada (b) elsewhere?
4.	How many pounds of wool, per fleece, can a musk-ox produce?
5.	What is the approximate number of musk-ox living in the wild state in Canada's northland?

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: DOMESTICATION OF MUSK-OX
speechtext:
1. Experiments in North America on the domestication 
of musk-oxen are being carried out at three localities. An American citizen has a small herd near Huntington Center, Vermont, which he obtained in 1954 and 1955, and a Canadian citizen has had a herd near Ardrossan, Alberta, since 1960. A third domestication experiment was initiated in 1964 under the auspices of the University of Alaska, at College, Alaska.
2.	(a) There are four musk-oxen in the Vermont herd, 19 in the Alberta herd and 23 in the University of Alaska herd, (b) The available information indicates only one calf has survived in the Vermont herd from those born since the capture of the parental stock. The Alberta herd produced one calf in 1962, three in 1963 and four in 1964, all surviving. No calves have yet been reported from the University of Alaska herd.
3.	(a) and (b) Domestication experiments are being carried on by private organizations and no costs to them are available except general statements that such costs are high.
4.	About six pounds of wool are produced annually by an adult musk-ox.
5.	About 10,000 musk-ox exist in the wild state in Canada today.

STUDIES OF INTERNATIONAL EXCHANGE PROPOSALS
STUDIES OF INTERNATIONAL EXCHANGE PROPOSALS
speechtext:
1.	What studies have been made by Canada of the international exchange of (a) Jacques Rueffl of France (b) Karl Blessing of West Germany (c) Walter S. Salant of United States?
2.	Has Canada made any analysis of the economic benefit to her, or otherwise, of a modified restoration of the gold standard and, if so, what conclusions have been reached?

speakeroldname: Mr. L. T. Pennell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: STUDIES OF INTERNATIONAL EXCHANGE PROPOSALS
speechtext:
1. Canada has been actively participating in studies and discussions in the International Monetary Fund and in the Group of Ten of a variety of proposals affecting the operation of the international exchange system. Some of these proposals have closely resembled those of Messrs. Rueff, Blessing and Salant. A technical sub-group (the Ossola Group) of the Group of Ten has been making studies of the possibilities with regard to supplementary reserve assets and it is expected to make its report to the Deputies of the Group of Ten in the near future. Canadian representatives are actively participating in the work of this sub-group.
2.	Yes. In a Ministerial statement of the Group of Ten released on the 10th of August, 1964, to which the Government of Canada 22620-87
fully subscribed, it was stated that "in reviewing the functioning of the international monetary system, the Ministers and Governors reaffirmed their conviction that a structure based, as the present is, on fixed exchange rates and the established price of gold, has proved its value as a foundation on which to build for the future". The major contribution to the stability to the international monetary system of the established price of gold was unanimously agreed by the representatives of the Governments which participate in the preparation of the report. Any change from present arrangements toward a closer adherence to a pure gold standard would not be welcomed by Canada.

MUNICIPAL CONSTRUCTION OF RESIDENCES FOR OLDER CITIZENS
speechtext: Can a municipality through the Winter Works Program construct a residence for older citizens and, if so, can the balance of the cost be obtained from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: MUNICIPAL CONSTRUCTION OF RESIDENCES FOR OLDER CITIZENS
speechtext:
A municipal residence for older citizens can qualify for the federal incentive payment under the Municipal Winter Works Incentive Program. Financing of such a municipal project by way of loans would not exclude it from the provisions of the program.

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Charles Canlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: PARK STEAMSHIP CORPORATION
speechtext:
The
Canadian Maritime Commission advises as follows:
1.	In actual practice the functions of Park Steamship Company at the time of its incorporation were the supervision, direction and control of the cargo vessels which were built by the Government for use during World War II. In the years intervening between the end of World War II and the present time, Park
Steamship Company Limited did not engage in active operations and its functions were limited to the administration of matters arising out of its earlier operations.
Arrangements are now under way for winding up the Company and surrendering its charter.
2.	Cargo ships which were assigned to the Company's fleet bore the names of various national and provincial parks in Canada, e.g., Banff Park, Laurentide Park, etc., and from this it is inferred that the name 'Park' was selected as a preliminary to the intended use of the names of such parks as ships' names.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I wish to rise on a point of order concerning written ques-

tions which have been placed on the order paper by Members for various reasons. In many cases they were directed to do so because of the type of information which is being sought. Any Member placing such question on the order paper, either on instructions or on his own initiative should, because of the urgency attached to them, be answered within 48 hours at most. But if we look over this order paper we find there are some 48 questions which are now six weeks old. There are approximately 11 which are five weeks old and approximately 60 which are three weeks old.
Surely the Government should pay attention to such matters as this if it wishes the oral question period to be shortened, bearing in mind that in certain circumstances a Member has no alternative but to place his question on the order paper. The most flagrant example of delay is provided by the starred questions. A starred question should be answered immediately. But three of these starred questions-Nos. 31, 44 and 65-have been on the order paper for six weeks. Either this situation is due to incompetence, or the Government is deliberately ignoring Members of the House by not answering these questions promptly.
I appeal to the Acting Prime Minister to direct this situation to the attention of his colleagues and bring about an expedition of the business of Parliament by ensuring that these questions are answered far more promptly than they have been up to now.

I would ask him this. Having regard to the espionage activities which involve at least two people and possibly others, would the Acting Prime Minister say whether it is the

intention of the Government to have charges pressed against the wrongdoers? Will the Government remove the veil of mystery surrounding these people and reveal their names? I asked for that the other day, and I ask the Minister now why should they enjoy the immunity of anonymity having allegedly committed an offence and received thousands of dollars unlawfully? Has the Government as yet decided whether a royal commission will be appointed to look into the whole field of espionage, wrongdoing and the ramifications thereof, some of which were left over from 1946 when a second spy ring remained uninvestigated?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LAYING OF CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity of reading the exchanges on this matter that took place when I was away. All I can say by way of supplement is that in any matter relating to security, particularly where activities by foreign agents are involved, it is extremely difficult to make information public without incurring the risk of compromising the measures that are constantly being taken to protect the safety and interests of Canada.
So far as the present case is concerned, more information has been given, I believe, than in any security case since 1946. But some aspects of the case are still under investigation. Anything that is said as to procedures or methods of handling such matters reveals information that may be useful to persons who are working against the interests of this country. In this regard I wish to remind the House of the practice it has always accepted in the past, that is to leave it to the administration in each individual case to decide how much information can safely be given in the interests of the country. The Government has come to the conclusion that in this case it must ask for the understanding of the House in declining to give any further information.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, May 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mcllraith (for the Prime Minister) for the second reading of Bill No. C-98, to make provision for the retirement of members of the Senate, and the proposed amendment of Mr. Howard.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF RETIREMENT AGE FOR SENATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as some hon. Members may recall, I rose to speak on the amendment just before five o'clock on Friday, and at that time I had no real opportunity to put forward my views in depth as to the merits of the amendment. But since hon. Members have had the week end to meditate upon the amendment which, as they will recall, provides that the bill be not now read a second time but that it be read this day six months hence, I think I need add little to my argument before suggesting we vote on it, and I feel sure most hon. Members will wish to support it.
I suggest that in our view, and in the view of those who in times past have expressed the desire that some reforms be made to the other place, the bill does so little that it is not really worth our support. That was one of the reasons I was urging hon. Members on
Division
Friday to support the amendment moved by my colleague from Skeena.
Before sitting down I would like to add a few words to indicate why, in my opinion, in western Canada there is less interest in and desire for the preservation of the Senate, and even for the attempt to improve and reform it, than apparently is the case in some other parts of the country. The main reason for this is quite apart from those advanced by the hon. Member for Skeena, when he suggested that the Liberal Party, and to a certain extent the Conservative Party, appear to have a built in interest in the perpetuation of the Senate.
In my view the reason there is so little interest in western Canada in the preservation or reform of the Senate is that it is not representative in any full measure of present day western Canada. Most of us are aware that the Senate, as it is presently constituted, has 24 members from Ontario, 24 from Quebec, 24 from three Maritime provinces, and only 24 from the four western provinces. It is one of two clauses in this amended version wherein I think we are departing from the principle of treating Members of both Houses alike in respect of pension and retirement matters. The last defence the Minister gave for this proposal was that some Senators would not have enough past service to provide for themselves a large enough pension to make it worth their while retiring. Of course, this is the problem of some Members of Parliament, too, and it is the problem of many Canadians; namely, to be able to provide for themselves an adequate pension.
I am not going into all of that matter at this point, much as I would like to; I would like to compare these pensions with what we are doing in the old age pension field generally.
But it does seem to me that it is wrong in principle to make a distinct difference between Members of the House of Commons and members of the Senate in this respect. When we brought in the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act we said to

the Members of this House of Commons that if they wished to do so, they could cover their past service. We are now saying to the members of the other place, "You cannot cover your past service, whether you want to or not". Of course, the effect of that with some Senators will be for them to stay away from the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act; they are going to elect to take the free pension of $8,000 at age 75. Mr. Chairman, I believe the simple answer is that the difference between Senators on appointment and Members of the House of Commons on election is not created by this bill. The difference of which the hon. Member speaks is really created by the fact that when an hon. Member is elected to this House he is elected with the certainty that his term of appoinment will not exceed five years. Then he may or may not submit himself to the electorate at the next general election. If he does, he may or may not be re-elected. On the other hand, when a Senator is summoned to the Senate he is summoned on an appointment for life with the fixed expectancy of holding his office in the other place. That is where the real difference lies. Therefore, because of that fundamental difference there is no way in which Members appointed in the past to the other place and Members elected to this place can be brought into identical relationship for the purpose of pensions benefits.
That being the case, it is then a matter of trying to work out what is the most equitable and fair way of dealing with the subject, so as to get a benefit which will try to keep as even a balance as can be kept between the Members of the House of Commons, newly appointed members of the Senate and members of the Senate appointed prior to

"To study the broad field of corrections, in its widest" sense, from the initial investigation of an offence through to the final discharge of a prisoner from imprisonment or parole, including such steps and measures as arrest, summonsing, bail, representation in Court, conviction, probation, sentencing, training, medical and psychiatric attention, release, parole, pardon, post release supervision and guidance and rehabilitation; to recommend as conclusions are reached, what changes, if any, should be made in the law and practice relating to these matters-

time from the first apprehension of the offender right through to his final release into the community free of any penal restraint whatsoever. Inevitably that committee will have to consider in a fundamental way principles of penology, including those upon which our present penal institutions and the Government plan for reform of them are founded. In the process of that consideration I think it can be expected that there will be comprehensive recommendations on that type of penal question.
I think hon. Members would, however, agree that in light of the conditions existing in some of our present maximum security institutions, of which the best known is St. Vincent de Paul, we do not have the option of postponing action in respect of the existing institutions until the expert committee can make its recommendations. There are urgent pressures now on the penitentiary service for more accommodation, apart altogether from the conditions existing in some of these institutions, and particularly in the one to which I have made reference.
I will illustrate this by reference to just a few statistics relating to institutions now under the control of the Government of Canada. In 1963 it was estimated that the institutions were overcrowded by 1,330 inmates, and it has been estimated that by 1967 there will be need for new accommodation for 2,560 inmates. The dictates of humanity alone argue for prompt action in making up this deficiency of physical accommodation, apart altogether from the fact that there is a requirement that more modern quarters be provided if a more modern system of correction is to be instituted, and if more modern theories and techniques of the correctional process are to be carried out in our institutions.
The purpose of this parliamentary committee on the other hand is to give Members of Parliament and, under the present terms of this resolution, members of the Senate, an opportunity to consider in greater detail both existing institutions and arrangements for discharging the Federal Government's responsibility in respect of maintaining prisons and, what may be even more important, to consider the present building program and future plans, which will enable the Government to discharge its duty in a better fashion.
The motion will also provide those in the corrections field, such as Members of the Canadian Corrections Association, various branches of the John Howard Society, the
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation Elizabeth Fry Society and organizations such as the Junior League Organization, which in recent years has taken such an active interest and participation in matters of correction, and groups representative of the various churches, an opportunity to comment on the proposed plan. Canadian Broadcasting Corporation Corporation to offer tree time to political parties.

Besides, I think that the Canadian people are entitled to that. Therefore, it is not a concession that the corporation must make, because the Canadian citizens have the right to receive information from political parties. often stretched, and the press, for propaganda purposes only.

Mr. Speaker, I think that it is my duty in the first place to set forth the present policy of the C.B.C. in this connection and then I will attempt to draw a few conclusions in regard to the C.B.C.'s policy as well as to motion now under consideration.
At present the C.B.C. gives generously on radio and television free time to recognized political parties, whenever it is required, both during election campaigns and between elections. Since there is no question at all of an election campaign for the time being, I feel sure that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency does not deal with free time allotted at election time but with free time given the year around to political parties.
The motion now before us refers to official political parties. Neither our constitution, that is the British North America Act, nor its amendments recognize official political parties. Nevertheless, there are political parties which are recognized as such in this house as well as, in some way, by the C.B.C. But from the constitutional point of view, they do not exist, and in order to know exactly which political parties will have free time on radio and television, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has set certain requirements which must be met by the various political parties concerned or by those who ask for free time.
The first requirement for a political party to be so recognized, is that the party must
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have policies on a wide range of national issues.
The second requirement is that the political party concerned must have a recognized national leader.
The third requirement is that the party must have a nation-wide organization established as the result of a national conference or convention.
The fourth requirement is that the political party in question must have representation in the House of Commons.
Finally, the fifth requirement, which only applies during an election campaign, provides that, to be recognized or entitled to free broadcasting time, a political party must seek the election of candidates in at least three of the provinces and put into the field at least one candidate for every four constituencies.
Generally those periods of free time are determined following a meeting attended by the leaders and representatives of the political parties, who try to come to an agreement. When these political parties cannot agree, the C.B.C. or, to be exact, the board of broadcast governors takes a decision, and that is exactly what happened on August 26, 1964, when the board of governors proposed the following allocation, which was accepted by four of the five political parties.

Member's motion, but I do not think most people in politics can get tremendously excited about the grievance that is implicit in the hon. Member's motion, not because there is not merit to it, but because it no longer seems to be that important.
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
It would seem to me that in terms of sheer time on radio and television on the C.B.C. during election time, it may still be important, and this is usually tied in a little more closely to the question of persons nominated and the representation in the previous House. It would seem that the tremendous audience build-up by private stations, as well as United States stations that can be seen either directly or through community antenna systems in Canada, has been largely instrumental in stripping the value from free time political broadcasts.
I think one other point that might be mentioned, is that the Government party has come up with the idea, which I understand is part of their program, that in future election expenses shall be subsidized to a certain extent by Parliament. That is one of the reasons this committee on election expenses is meeting in respect of the media of radio, and particularly television. That seems to me to be the main reason that politicians, particularly Members of the majority party, are prepared to look at this tremendously high cost of an election campaign, particularly in respect of spot messages in this country with so many stations, and as varied a number of media, through which one must advertise to get some kind of saturation. It seems to me that if we arrive in the next couple of years at successful legislation in line with this particular policy, as has happened in Quebec, even more of the value will be removed from this sharing of free time television.
The hon. Member's motion would be appreciated more if it included some requirement regarding private stations, because the private stations are under the jurisdiction of the Board of Broadcast Governors, and the Lord knows that each one of them when making an application for a licence has given lip service to the idea of public service, and has always been prepared to argue this very fully. The hon. Member's motion would have had a bit more point had it expressed more directly his own party's grievance.
With that comment, Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mcllraith (for Mr. Favreau):
That a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons be appointed to consider the state of penitentiaries under the control of the Government of Canada and the plans of the government in relation thereto with powers to report from time to time its observations and opinions thereon; send for persons, papers and records; adjourn from place to place; sit during sittings of the House; and print from day to day such papers and evidence as may be ordered by the committee, and that standing order 66 be suspended in relation thereto;
That 15 members of the House of Commons, to he designated at a later date, act on behalf of the House as Members of the said committee; and
That a Message be sent to the Senate requesting that House to unite with this House for the above purpose, and to select, if the Senate deem advisable, some of their Members to act on the proposed joint committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I had made reference to the fact that in conjunction with the committee which it is proposed to set up under this resolution, the Government has already taken steps to establish a Committee of Inquiry headed by Mr. Justice Ouimet of Montreal, along with a number of other distinguished citizens interested in the field of study of a proper system of corrections in Canada. I had made reference also to the fact that it is the Government's wish that this parliamentary committee should take full advantage of the opportunity to examine the existing penal institutions in Canada and also examine in full the construction program which is now under way, as well as the Government's plans for development of penal institutions.
Perhaps by way of establishing principles I might make reference first to the following quotation to indicate some of the criteria upon which penal institutions are based. I quote:
There are three classes of prison inmates: the accidental or occasional criminal, the reformable criminal, and the habitual or persistent offender. Those included in the first two categories always return to freedom, those of the last category, with few exceptions, should never be set at liberty. The great majority of prisoners will be called upon at some time to live again the ordinary life of a free man. Therefore, entirely apart from humanitarian grounds, and from a purely economic point

of view and for the eventual benefit of society, the task of the prison should be not merely the temporary protection of society through the incarceration of captured offenders, but the transformation of reformable criminals into law abiding citizens, and the prevention of those who are accidental or occasional criminals from becoming habitual offenders.
The source of the quotation goes on to refer to the fact that, generally speaking, the accidental or occasional criminal is generally rehabilitated back into society, and then remarks:
The reformable criminal, the youthful offender, the first offender or even the second or third offender will not be reformed if, during his term in prison his spirit has been broken, his habit of industry (if it ever existed) suppressed, and his morals corrupted by prison associations. He has been guilty of a crime, and it is inevitable that he should suffer, but society should not weaken its structure, nor incur large and excessive expenditure, by turning him out no better, or even worse, than when he entered a penal institution.
The process of penal treatment for the two first named categories of criminals, and to a certain but less extent for the last, must be directed unceasingly to the advancement of the individual's personal and emotional rehabilitation.
I would think no one could take exception to the particular quotation on this subject matter, particularly in view of the fact it is a quotation from the Archambault Commission report on penal institutions in Canada made nearly 30 years ago, in 1938. It is the hope of the Government that the penal system of Canada can be brought into close conformity to the principles set out in the passage which I have quoted. The committee study will enable Members to have access, at first hand, to the Government's advisers on this matter in order to determine the manner in which those principles have been worked out, and as well to examine the institutions themselves and see at first hand the procedures being followed within the institutions leading to that objective.
In carrying out these objectives, the committee will be able to make an appraisal of the capital stock of the institutions which we have on hand and which are now available to carry out this process of rehabilitation. I should like to repeat a remark I made this afternoon, that it would be preferable to start off, a priori, with a system of correction which could be planned from the start, unhampered by any restrictions from the past such as existing buildings. However, the realities of the situation require that existing physical assets be utilized so far as possible, with changes in existing plant being made to make them suitable to the objectives.
May 17. 1965

Starting therefore with an assessment of the existing tools which are available, this Government's conclusion has been that the present facilities are not adequate to carry out a comprehensive program of rehabilitation. It is because of this inadequacy that the Government has proposed, as an initial step, an extensive program of institutional construction. It has already been pointed out earlier, but I would repeat today within this context, that within the next ten years it is proposed to furnish each regional penitentiary district with the following basic facilities: A reception centre; a special detention unit; a maximum security unit; medium and minimum security facilities; a psychiatric unit as well as hospital facilities; pre-release facilities; a staff training college. Perhaps I might pause for a moment and refer to a number of these categories, these types of institution, just to emphasize the importance they have in our correctional system.
I might start first in time, and I would suggest first in logic, with the reception centre itself, for it is into this institution that the offender is first received from the courts, and it is in this institution that the process of classification, the process of determining the type of rehabilitation and reform treatment that should be given to him, is to be carried out by the qualified professional staff. This institution is the very keystone of the correctional system. In one of our penitentiary districts at least, that is in the Ontario district of Kingston, the experience has been that the offenders who come in from the courts and are mixed in with maximum security prisoners, with no possibility of segregation and no possibility of consideration of the new inmates from the standpoint of classification alone.
The institutions for young offenders have drawn much attention from many Members of the House and members of the public in recent years. The institutions which the Government proposes are for young offenders between the ages of 16 and 25. These will be institutions in which they can be detained apart from, shall we say, the hard core criminals, and institutions which will be primarily engaged in retraining these young offenders so that they might find a useful place again in society. The hospitals which will be built will naturally include medical facilities for, after all, special medical problems are created where you have a large community of people who are under detention. I should like to emphasize particularly the Government's intention to develop better psychiatric facili-
Penitentiaries Committee ties to deal with those problems which are at times more medical than problems of criminal law.
Finally, a novelty at the federal level in Canada although not a novelty in the civilized world, is the Government's intention to establish pre-discharge centres, centres which will enable prisoners who are shortly to be released into society to overcome the disadvantages they have had from the process of incarceration and living in an unnatural regime away from society.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Ultimately the prisoner must go on his own when he goes back into society, but it is felt at the present time that the process of adjustment from within the prison walls, out into the community, is too drastic, and these pre-discharge centres will enable the individual to adjust himself better to the first few months in society, which are the most critical for him, in order to avoid his again becoming an inmate of the prison.
I should now like to make reference to some of the physical construction going on at the present time. A special detention unit is now being constructed in connection with the B.C. penitentiary. Three more will be constructed in future years at Dorchester in New Brunswick, St. Vincent de Paul and-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
What are you asking the question for, then? I was referring to the fact that special detention units are to be built at Dorchester, New Brunswick, at St. Vincent de Paul and as part of the Mill-haven complex to be constructed at Kingston. A maximum security institution is to be built at Ste. Anne des Plaines, Quebec, and another as part of the Millhaven complex. At the present time there are four medium security institutions under construction at Cowansville, Quebec, Springhill, in Nova Scotia, Warkworth in Ontario, and Drumheller, Alberta. In addition there is approaching completion a special drug addiction centre at Matsqui, B.C.
While buildings are important, and so is having the right environment in which to carry out the correctional processes, they are no more important in successful rehabilitation than having competent staff available to carry out the classification and training of inmates. The Canadian penitentiary service has already instituted a program of induction training for penitentiary staff when they first come into the service, and supplementary staff courses for more senior personnel as they go on to take greater responsibilities within the service.
In this connection the Alderwood staff college was opened at Kingston last fall, and existing facilities have been converted to the same use at St. Vincent de Paul and New Westminster. An entirely new staff training college will be commenced in connection with St. Vincent de Paul.
By 1973 this plan proposes, as I have said, to have available in each penitentiary district specialized institutions which will enable a complete process of classification of offenders to take place, and will provide more versatile means of giving treatment according to classification. Since the committee will hear in some detail the Government's proposals in this regard, particularly with respect to new construction, I do not propose to elaborate further on those this evening.
I would in passing, however, like to make reference to one important facet in penology which at the moment is not entirely under the control of the Federal Government, and

that is the establishment of effective probation systems. Probation has a great potential in respect of the Canadian penal system. Probation, might I say for the benefit of hon. Members not familiar with it, is the process whereby in sentencing an offender the magistrate in effect suspends sentence, and instead of putting the prisoner in an institution lets him out in society under the supervision of a probation officer.
The probation officer serves a valuable function for the magistrates and the courts deciding on criminal cases, by providing what is really an initial step in classification, giving the magistrate a pre-sentence report on a particular offender so that the magistrate in turn may be better informed in the course of passing sentence.
A problem has existed in this respect arising out of the nature of our constitution. We in this federal legislature have in our control over the Criminal Code the power of determining under what conditions and at what times the presiding judge or magistrate may suspend sentence. The provincial authorities on the other hand have the responsibility for maintaining probation officers. I would suggest, and I offer this as a personal opinion, that there is great scope for development at both levels. In this connection perhaps I might again refer to the Archambault Report which states at page 8:
The system must start at the source, and fight the cause before the effect. It is admitted that, once a child or youth has had experience of prison, his subsequent reformation is extremely doubtful.
This is the technique which has been very usefully applied in the U.K., and it is something which has application to Canada, because it is a fact that the prison population in the United Kingdom is much less per capita than in Canada, particularly because of their very enlightened and extensive use of probation and parole. The committee under Mr. Justice Ouimet is going to study and report on this particular question, and I would submit it is one of the most important questions on which it can decide and make recommendations to the Government.
I pointed out earlier that it might well be objected that the Government should not be pressing on with a construction program at this time while the principles are being studied and recommended upon by the Ouimet committee.

But I would point out to my hon. friend that we cannot in all con-
May 17. 1965

science detain men in the bucket cells in Dorchester and St. Vincent de Paul one second longer than is necessary to provide new quarters. And to delay the construction of better facilities in which to segregate and offer training to juvenile offenders is to risk continual additions to the population of hard core criminal offenders.
It is the Government's intention that penitentiary policy shall be flexible and eclectic. Changes in the policy will be made whenever necessary, founded upon both our own experience and the counsel and experience of people active in the corrections field. I would like to emphasize the flexible nature of the approach by the Government in this regard, and in fact it is hoped the committee will find it possible to make early interim reports on the various matters which will be the subject of its studies, and these will be taken fully into account in penitentiary planning.
I would suggest that by embarking at once upon a program to eliminate the results of long years of neglect of our penal institutions, and to put them in a position to carry out modem concepts of rehabilitation, we can make of them instruments for reducing the criminal population of this country, and to restore public confidence in the humanity and justice of our corrections system.
One of the great measurements of a country's degree of civilization is surely the compassion and wisdom with which it treats not only the normal law-abiding citizen but the abnormal citizen, the lawbreaker. One of the most important studies this Parliament can make is the subject matter of this resolution which I hope will be accepted very early by the House.

course, Mr. Speaker, any program which will move another step along the path blazed in penal reform by the former Minister of Justice, Hon. E. Davie Fulton, will be welcomed not only by my colleagues in this party but I am sure by all people in Parliament and throughout the country. I think it is well at this stage, when we are setting up a committee to look into plans which apparently are already made, that we should remind ourselves that unless penal reform has widespread support in Parliament, and also the support of editorial writers and the general public, it is bound to get bogged down in threats and complaints about mollycoddling and other such easy answers which uniformed people like to give in this particular field of human reform and endeavour.
Penitentiaries Committee [DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I think it is a pity that it is May, 1965, when we are considering this resolution. It was May 22, 1964, when the Minister of Justice speaking in Vancouver outlined several plans he had, and it is a shame a committee has not had a year to look over the plans of the various institutions, the construction of which has been outlined by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister. I do not know who is to be on the committee when it is set up, but I am sure its members would like to hear the complaints of the Canadian Corrections Association about the alleged fortress which is to be built in St. Vincent de Paul. Having said that, obviously some reform of the outmoded facilities has to be made in this area. But I think the committee should have an opportunity to investigate very carefully a concept which seems to a good many knowledgeable people in this field a concept which is very much outmoded in these days. The Canadian Corrections Association has a set of standards for present consideration. I will not repeat them; they will be found in Hansard.
Some time back this House debated the proposed move of the women's prison at Kingston to the City of Cornwall. I assume that this proposal has been pigeonholed. If this is not the case, the committee or a good many of its Members will have some interesting questions to ask. I have had for a year in my files the Government return of complaints about the move of the women's prison. I do not expect to have to use them, but reading them over it is evident that a much closer liaison will have to be established between the Commissioner and his staff, the other advisers of the Department of Justice and the various volunteer agencies in the prison, parole and probation field. For instance, according to a statement from the Elizabeth Fry Society of Kingston the Commissioner had indicated that before any major change of policy was made a representative group of the directors and others interested in this work would have an opportunity to make a presentation to the Commissioner and the committee. Instead, an announcement was made without any reference to any of these societies, which do such wonderful work.
I am glad to see that the hon. Member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) is present. I hope the committee will have an opportunity to review the implications of a speech he made about moving prisoners to strategic locations in the Canadian North. If I did not know

May 17. 1965
Penitentiaries Committee the hon. Member and have great respect for him I would think this speech had been made not 100 years ago, but 150 years ago. This is the type of policy which led years ago to the establishment of Australia. I hope the Government's imagination with regard to a forward-looking policy for the North does not stop with this narrow and outmoded thinking.
The Fredericton Gleaner in an editorial on May 15, 1965 commented as follows under the headline "Shades of Siberia".
The similarity of climate between Canada and Russia is a geophysical fact which neither country can escape. But so far there has been an understandable reluctance on Canada's part to go in for any corresponding duplication in institutions.
At least until now. Mr. John R. Matheson (L-Leeds) has a bill on the Commons order paper which would emulate one of the most ancient of Russian customs, far antedating communism, the sending of people to Siberia.
Mr. Matheson suggests that criminals, particularly those who seem to have the best chance for rehabilitation, should be sent not to the penitentiary but to "minimum security work camps at strategic locations in the Canadian Arctic."
There they would work at the construction of air strips, harbours, and other installations calculated to serve economic, scientific and other national interests.
The article ends:
Well, it's an idea, even if the Russians did think of it first.
I am sure there will be an opportunity for us to hear the hon. Member for Leeds discussing this policy. Perhaps he can appear before the committee on penitentiaries and give the committee the benefit of his modern opinions of penal reform.
There is one point I should like to make. The whole point of minimum security institutions is, of course, their accessibility to members of the public so that they can come to visit the inmates of these institutions and in order that the inmates can play some role, a minor one I admit, in the society where they happen to be located. I have learned a little about the great Canadian North. It is axiomatic that anyone who is a supporter of this party should know something about the North: It is part of us. I do not think many inmates of these prisons would have much interchange from a family point of view with residents in the Northwest Territories or the Yukon. That is admittedly a minor consideration, it is true, but we are humanitarians here and we must keep all these factors in mind.
Members in all parties support sane and sensible measures of reform. I should like to read into the record a paragraph or two from an editorial which appeared in the Toronto

Globe and Mail on Friday, May 22, 1964. It shows we have been waiting in the wings as far as these penitentiaries are concerned- waiting for the Government to reach a dramatic conclusion that a committee of this House and the other place should be set up to consider the state of the penitentiaries. Well, we have had our gestation period, now. We have reached the point of setting up our 22-man committee. The article is headed The Purpose of Prisons and it reads:
Canada has for a long time needed to know the purpose for which her prisons exist. Three purposes have generally been given lip service: they exist to take society's revenge upon criminals for their antisocial acts; they exist to deter would-be criminals; they exist to convert criminals into useful citizens.
The trouble with this multi-purpose approach is that revenge and deterrence are not compatible, in the same institution, with rehabilitation.
I know the Parliamentary Secretary will agree with this premise:
It is psychologically almost impossible to reform a man while treating him vengefully and holding him up as a bad example. Yet reformation should be the end we seek to achieve, not only for humanitarian reasons but because in the long run it is cheaper for a society to reform its criminals than to perpetuate them in crime.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I will interpolate here for a moment. When I used to have other responsibilities in this field, people would say to me: "You are being too easy on prisoners." And they would discuss the probation system, and so on. It is amazing how criticism will dissolve when you point out to people who are not moved by other considerations, considerations of humanity and other things, that it is much cheaper to have a good rehabilitation program. Then suddenly people get the message and become ardent reformers. This field has been whipped and given lip service for more years than I know most people in this House would like to think about.
Speaking for my party, Mr. Speaker, we welcome the setting up of the committee. We hope that the committee will have an opportunity-and I think I heard the Parliamentary Secretary aright when he said they would-to view the plans, even though they are well advanced now, for the various institutions that are to be built. I end where I started, by saying that any program involving reform in this very important area of human progress needs the enthusiastic and informed support of Members of Parliament and also the news media of our country. With that combination I think the committee can do a very useful job for the country.
May 17, 1965

The Parliamentary Secretary mentioned the constitutional problem. I agree that there is a constitutional problem, but I do not think it is insurmountable. I believe this is an area where there can be, and the public would expect, very close co-operation between the jurisdictions. I suspect that the committee- and it says here, "to consider the state of penitentiaries . . . and the plans of the Government in relation thereto"-would be very interested in the close connection that exists in regard to prisoners awaiting trial or other judicial processes. Of course, who could forget the case of the missing Lucien Rivard, who apparently has been able to go to some other part of the world.

I think this is an area- and I am being very serious, Mr. Speaker- where a very much closer liaison between the two jurisdictions could very profitably be set up. If such a liaison had existed before Mr. Rivard needed to flood that skating rink on the memorable day when the temperature was 42 degrees, perhaps he would not have escaped. Mr. Speaker, the resolution is a very direct one and it should not take a very long time to organize the committee. Speaking for this party, I say that we welcome the establishment of the committee.
