Mr. Speaker, I am certain we have all listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Macdonald) in introducing the resolution which is now before us for discussion. I know we all welcome the interest of the Government in giving consideration and thought to the question of penology as it now exists in Canada. Anyone who has made any study of penology, who has visited the penitentiaries and the prison systems of our country, I am certain will have to admit that Canada is one of the most backward countries in the world in the introduction and establishment of modern penology. I think there are two reasons for this. One is the method of escapism in the past; in appointing royal commissions and committees of inquiry, receiving the reports and then not doing anything about the recommendations contained in those reports.
I was most interested when the Parliamentary Secretary on two occasions at least quoted, and quoted with commendation, certain remarks in the Archambault Report. I most certainly agree with those quotations. But I am referring to the Archambault Report-1938. And recommendation after recommendation in the Archambault Report I am convinced will be to some extent the same recommendations that will come down from the two committees which are to work in the next year or two. There has been an absolute neglect by successive governments in taking under consideration the advice of the royal commissions they have appointed to undertake certain responsibilities.
That, of course, must be added to by the attitude of past Ministers of Finance in just not giving a hoot about the penitentiaries or the penitentiary system and not recognizing that they were being penny wise and pound foolish, because although there will be and has been a requirement for millions of dollars of expenditures on new types of jail construction, the fact is that right today it costs $2,750 a year to keep an inmate in a penitentiary. Yet past governments have been satisfied just to continue on the basis of a system of penology based on retribution, instead of the dual principles of the protection of society and the rehabilitation of the antisocial individual who had to be incarcerated, under the laws of our country, in our jails and penitentiaries.
1382	COMMONS
Penitentiaries Committee [DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
However, Mr. Speaker, I must admit that even after the lengthy and interesting introduction of this resolution by the Parliamentary Secretary, I am still puzzled as to what is the policy-thinking of the Government on the studies into the system of Canadian penology, with a view to bringing forward their recommendations. I still have not got clear the basis of the thinking of the Government regarding the need, the requirement and the efficiency of the appointment of two commissions. Some days ago we had the announcement of the appointment of a Royal Commission consisting of four members. These four are to be given all the technical assistance they require and will have advisory committees from associations in Canada who have a great interest in the knowledge of penology and our penitentiaries system. But, Mr. Speaker, just look at the terms of reference of the Royal Commission, to be found at page 208 of Hansard, which have now been approved by the Cabinet. The terms of reference of this special committee on correctional reform are as follows:
To study the broad field of corrections, In its widest sense, from the initial investigation of an offence through to the final discharge of a prisoner from imprisonment or parole, including such steps and measures as arrest, summonsing, bail, representation in Court, conviction, probation, sentencing, training, medical and psychiatric attention, release, parole, pardon, post release supervision and guidance and rehabilitation;-
Then in case not everything was included they also have the authority in their terms of reference to consider and recommend upon any matters necessarily ancillary to the foregoing. So this Royal Commission has been appointed and those are its terms of reference.
I take that under its ancillary powers will be the question of construction.
I have had, Mr. Speaker, an interest in penology for some 30 years now, from the outside looking in, being able to get in but always able to get out. I do not understand how you can separate the principles of modern penology from the type of construction of our jails. I do not understand how you can discuss rehabilitation of an inmate inside the four walls so that he is transformed into a better citizen outside unless you take into consideration the construction of those walls and what is inside them. Therefore I take it that this Royal Commission which was appointed a few weeks ago has to tie in its lengthy terms of reference with this question of construction, and make recommendations upon any matters affecting our penitentiaries,

DEBATES	May 17, 1965
right from the time of arrest of prisoners to post-parole and post-release care.
If that thinking is correct, then on what basis does the Government now introduce a resolution recommending the appointment of a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons, composed of 15 members of this House, without the powers or terms of references of the Royal Commission that has been appointed, but dealing with construction the existing state of affairs, and to study the Government's plans, which on a construction basis the Parliamentary Secretary has stated is a 10 year plan? How can you logically and releasably speak of modern penology, of modern thinking from the time of arrest to postrelease, and then as a fait accompli announce a 10 year plan of construction? I know it is in existence because I have seen a model in a building about two blocks from here. It just does not make sense to me, and I hope that before this motion comes to a decision we will have further explanation from somebody on the Government side of the House.
I also hope there will be a clarification of the terms of reference of Government Order No. 10. All that is proposed is that a Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons be appointed to consider the state of penitentiaries under the control of the Government of Canada, etc., etc. But what is meant by the "state of penitentiaries"? If it means the state of them as related to the provision of temporary needs, then there may be some purpose in the appointment of this committee. But if that is all it means, then it is not good enough. I should like to know whether the "state of penitentiaries" applies to the training now going on in penitentiaries, and to the wages and responsibilities of employees in the penitentiaries service. If that is what is meant, then perhaps there may be an argument for this type of parliamentary committee, which could deal with matters of immediate concern, if the recommendations of such committee received immediate action and if they dealt with more than building but also, as I say, with personnel, with training, and with certain dangerous situations which presently exist.
As an illustration, may I express the hope that this committee will deal with the matter of personnel. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that whomsoever it was, either individual or committee, who arranged the last increase for the personnel of the penitentiaries system in Canada, he or it did not have the foggiest notion of the penitentiaries service or
May 17, 1965

Penitentiaries Committee
the responsibilities of those in the various categories in the penitentiaries system. Because of this the decisions taken were not only just out of this world, but in many cases unjust, and they have led to a breakdown in the morale of those in the penitentiaries service.
Just to illustrate what I mean, Mr. Speaker, the clerks did not get an increase. The reason was because they were receiving the same pay, or a bit more, than clerks in other services; and the attitude of Treasury Board is that a clerk is a clerk no matter where he works. May I point out that a clerk in a penitentiary is entirely different from a clerk outside a penitentiary, because he is in contact with convicts, with antisocial persons. In addition to that, under the regulations of the penitentiaries service a clerk has major responsibility in the event of a riot. But no, they say a clerk is a clerk so no increase in wages was granted.
There was also no increase for messengers. This, Mr. Speaker, was a honey. Messengers in the penitentiaries service received no increase because Treasury Board said they were messengers and should get the same as messengers in the Government service. They do not come in contact with the inmates. Let me point out that a man driving a truck into a jail is in contact with inmates, so he gets a raise. A messenger is responsible for every inmate and has to sign for each one when he takes them out of a penitentiary to a hospital or a court. He carries a side-arm and is solely responsible, but he is classified as a messenger so he gets no increase. If matters of this nature can be studied under the terms of reference of this committee, then I think there may be some advantage.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I should like to know whether one other matter will fall within the interpretation of the phrase "state of penitentiaries". Will the special committee have authority to interview inmates to obtain their opinions as to the state of the penitentiaries? These people live in these places, or at least exist in them, and some of them have definite ideas as to conditions. If the committee will have the authority to interview these inmates, I suggest it will be a busy committee, because on the second last occasion I visited the British Columbia Penitentiary there were 70 applications from inmates for interviews, and it took me three and a half days to complete those interviews in that one penitentiary. I might add that it took me about five weeks
to look into their problems. Will this authority exist within an interpretation of "state of penitentiaries"? We have not been told about these things.
Will the committee under its terms of reference have the authority to look into what I termed a few minutes ago as "dangerous situations" and make recommendations in that regard? As of April 27 of this year there was overcrowding in the British Columbia Penitentiary and its satellites, including the minimum security prison at Williams Head and the farm at Agassiz. There are 1,006 inmates in the British Columbia penitentiary system. There are 83 inmates who are in there for sex offences of a nominal nature. There are 13 classified as dangerous sexual offenders. There are also 13 inmates serving life sentences, and 46 who were committed as habitual criminals. All told, there are 90 inmates in the one penitentiary who have nothing to lose: They are there for life. The conditions under which they live are overcrowded and they have nothing to do. I spoke recently with the regional warden, Mr. Hall, and another warden, Mr. Moloney. They both tell me they are extremely nervous about the situation. They had a serious riot there not too long ago. In view of the number of habitual criminals serving indeterminate sentences and the number serving life sentences who have nothing to lose, considering the terrible conditions, it is more than likely that serious trouble will break out again, in time.
Will this committee under its terms of reference, and within the meaning of "the state of penitentiaries", have the authority to look into these matters which cannot be dealt with except on a long term basis by the Royal Commission? If that is what the Government has in mind, then perhaps there is some basis for the argument to set up a Parliamentary committee as well as the Royal Commission, with broad terms of reference covering every possible field of penology.
I do not think I need say more, but I do hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will clarify the basic policy thinking of the Government in respect of the appointment of these two bodies, and at the same time explain in depth the meaning of the terms of reference, particularly that three word phrase "state of penitentiaries" as it appears in resolution No. 10.
In conclusion I should like to express my heartfelt wish that the Royal Commission and the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and

May 17. 1965
Penitentiaries Committee the House of Commons will do a complete and thorough job, will present worth-while recommendations which, keeping our fingers crossed, the Government will not treat in the same manner as another Government treated the Archambault Report of 1938, the recommendations of which have not yet been acted upon.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in respect of resolution No. 10 now before the House, we note the Government's intention, in proposing the setting up of a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, to consider the state of penitentiaries under the control of the Government. I do not believe there is any disagreement in any part of this House as to the need for something to be done, and perhaps this joint committee, in conjunction with the Royal Commission which has been set up by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), can get on with the job, make studies and bring in recommendations as quickly as possible so that the Government can act on those resolutions as quickly as possible.
I should like to state on behalf of the party to which I belong that we join with those who are concerned about the lack of action on the part of previous governments in respect of recommendations made by various commissions set up in respect of penal reform. We agree with the Parliamentary Secretary that one of the objectives of this study should be the reduction of the criminal population in Canadian penitentiaries. We also agree that we should adopt a far more modem outlook in considering the matter of rehabilitation.
On behalf of this party let me say that we do not adopt the view that all of the plans for construction should be held in abeyance until the reports of these two inquiring bodies have been received. We can no longer tolerate the overcrowding in our penitentiaries across Canada. What is more, we can no longer tolerate the substandard or subacceptable accommodation which exists at this time in many parts of Canada. The hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) has just referred to an overcrowded situation in the penitentiary in British Columbia, and we have heard a great deal about the overcrowding and the low standard of accommodation in St. Vincent de Paul. In view of these circumstances, it is not our belief that we should advocate a policy of holding in abeyance the construction of new accommodation, particularly when we realize that some of the very old and outdated below standard situations, which are

not acceptable in this day and age, have been the subject of reports by several royal commissions in the past, including the one that reported in 1938 and the one that reported in 1956, on penal and rehabilitation reform.
We hope that all construction now planned over the ten year period, amounting to something in the neighbourhood of $100 million, will not be held up. We hope also that the people who made these plans were guided by some of the recommendations presented to the Government by other royal commissions. I suggest to the Parliamentary Secretary that perhaps the plans should be modified during the course of the ten year construction period in accordance with new recommendations which may be made by the Royal Commission announced on April 9, and the Joint Committee of the House and the Senate.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps we should be prepared to go a little bit further than making a study at this time as to what the problems are with respect to the rehabilitation and treatment of convicts. We could probably take a lesson from the British Government which, I understand, has set up a continuing committee of experts, people who are well trained, to keep their penal reform institutions modernized, not only in the administration and application of the law but also in connection with post-release treatment that offenders require if they are going to take their place in society.
The terms of reference of the Royal Commission which was set up can be found on page 208 of Hansard, and includes such things as the representation in court, conviction, probation, sentencing and so on. A few days ago we had a very interesting, and I hope useful debate during the private Members' hour with regard to legal aid. I am very happy to inform those Members who have not been informed already that in the Province of Alberta, a committee for legal aid has been established in each one of our major cities. I know that the branch of the Law Society in my own city met and set up the conditions and regulations as well as responsibilities of each member of the Law Society in that city with regard to this matter of legal aid. Even though the Federal Government has failed to move rapidly in this very important field, some of the provinces as well as the Province of Alberta about which I am particularly informed, have moved ahead, so that people who have been charged are given the necessary assistance of the legal profession for
May 17, 1965

which they are not able to pay. It can be argued that this is a provincial responsibility in the first instance. I would hope that the Federal Government also would assume some of this responsibility to make certain that people are not going to be wrongly accused or And it difficult to defend themselves as a result of lack of funds.
I am not going to talk longer on this matter. We in this party generally support the resolution. We hope that the joint committee will be successful in bringing in plans and recommendations that can be accepted and implemented by the Government very quickly. We share in the wish that has been expressed by the hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and the hon. Member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather), that there will be no undue delay in giving effect to the recommendations after they are introduced.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
In rising to make a contribution with regard to this Government motion, I should like to suggest that one of the most effective ways of stirring the public conscience on a matter of such great importance is to conduct a public inquiry or, as has been proposed here, set up a Committee of this House which can actually study the state of our penitentiaries. I recall that the Archambault Commission was appointed in 1936 specifically to study the prison system. Later, in 1953, a still more influential committee was appointed under the chairmanship of Hon. Mr. Justice Gerald Fauteux, to study the remission services of the Department of Justice.
Now, in actual fact both committees wandered oyer a broader field than that which was assigned to them. I do not believe we have any need to be concerned that there will be any tendency on the part of any people in authority to limit or curtail the useful examination by the parliamentary committee on the state of our penitentiaries. I am assured of this, Sir, having read eight statements, provocative and scholarly, which have been delivered by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). I am mindful of the fact that during his tenure of office Hon. Davie Fulton made quite a number of speeches on this subject. I believe I have read every speech that he made on penology just as I have read every speech which has been made by the present Minister of Justice.
Perhaps hon. Members would be interested in reviewing what the Minister of Justice has said specifically on this subject. I have studied these speeches with great
Penitentiaries Committee care. I have been unable to find one sentence, not to say one paragraph, in any speech which I think is political in tone. The first was an address to the John Howard Society in Vancouver, May 20, 1964. This was followed by an address to the Association of Police Chiefs of the Province of Quebec, in Quebec City on June 9, 1964. The Minister then spoke to the New York State Probation Officers Association and the Ontario Probation Officers Association in Niagara Falls on October 8, 1964. There was then an address to La Societe Canadienne de Criminologie in Montreal, November 5, 1964. Hon. Members will recall, too, his contribution on the departmental estimates under the subject of penitentiaries in the House of Commons under date of November 23, 1964. The Minister then addressed the John Howard Society of Nova Scotia at Halifax on February 4, 1965. The Minister made the important announcement in the House of Commons of a Special Committee on Corrections on April 9, 1965. His last contribution of which I am aware has been to the John Howard Society of Ontario at Osgoode Hall, Toronto, on April 27, 1965.
These addresses cover a wide range. I think every one of them is worthy of examination by all people seriously interested in the Minister's attitude with respect to the purpose of prisons and toward penological reform. Perhaps the most important question before us is this old question of the purpose of prisons. I refer hon. Members to an editorial appearing in the Globe and Mail for Friday, May 22, 1964 in which the editor under the title of The Purpose of Prisons, says:
Canada has for a long time needed to know the purpose for which her prisons exist. Three purposes have generally been given lip service: they exist to take society's revenge upon criminals for their antisocial acts; they exist to deter would-be criminals; they exist to convert criminals into useful citizens.
The trouble with this multi-purpose approach is that revenge and deterrence are not compatible in the same institution, with rehabilitation. It is psychologically almost impossible to reform a man while treating him vengefully and holding him up as a bad example. Yet reformation should be the end we seek to achieve, not only for humanitarian reasons but because in the long run it is cheaper for a society to reform its criminals than to perpetuate them in crime.
The hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) referred to the fact it costs us something in the order of $2,750 to keep a prisoner in a penitentiary for one year. This, of course, does not take into account the added
1386	COMMONS
Penitentiaries Committee burden on society generally of maintaining this man's family, his wife, his children and perhaps in later years successive generations of criminals.
The Minister of Justice indicated in some of his speeches that the purely negative, vindictive technique of our penal system seems less likely in the long run to protect society than to expose it to assaults ever more vicious.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
This is borne out by the fact that 85 per cent of our people in federal institutions are recidivists. In the long run punishment promises society no real security. The only lasting way to prevent trouble is surely reformation, if such is possible. The ideas of punishment and rehabilitation meet in a single aim, to protect the community. Therefore all Canadians are interested in a fresh approach of how to deal with these socially disturbed people who are contributing great hurt to themselves, their families and to society generally. We cannot regard this question in any soft or sentimental way because it is manifest that crime is on the increase.
I have been disturbed that the Government does not appear to have very ready access to some of the statistics on this subject or, if it has, they have not been made available. I refer, for example, to question No. 35 on the Order Paper which asks the number of crimes remaining unsolved per one hundred thousand of the population during the last five years, the percentage increase in Canada's population, and in the population of federal penitentiaries. I know penologists in Canada have been quite exercised with respect to the lack of adequate statistics, and I would refer in this connection to the report of the third criminal law conference held at Osgoode Hall, on April 3 and 4, 1964, and to a contribution by M. L. Friedland and J. W. Mohr appearing in The Criminal Law Quarterly.
It would appear clear to those who have full access to the facts that crime in the United States is out of hand. My own judgment, from what I have been able to read, is that crime in Canada is sharply on the increase. Indictable offences have increased way out of proportion to the increase in population.
It is clear juvenile delinquency is also on the increase, and as well it is clear that only a fragment of reported crime ever results in conviction, something of the order of 40 per cent. The fact is that although Canada has one of the highest prison popula-
[Mr. Matheson.l
DEBATES	May 17, 1965
tions of any civilized country, crime is tending to increase here. Therefore I am not urging anything that may be regarded as soft.
To me it is a shocking fact that in Canada a first offender statistically receives a longer sentence than a man who has been in prison on several occasions. At the present time the average first offender in a federal institution has a sentence of something in excess of 3.5 years. Surely many of these people should never have been sent to prison in the first instance but should have been treated in some other way.
The other day, on May 12, 1965, when we had a discussion with respect to the very interesting bill proposed by the Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), a member of the Ontario Bar who has earned the esteem of all trial lawyers in Ontario, I referred to part of an address by the Rev. S. G. West, Director of the Anglican Correctional Chaplaincy. Rev. Mr. West has pointed out that a Canadian has approximately eight times the likelihood of ending up in prison than a person who resides in Holland, in the Scandinavian countries or in the United Kingdom, and pointedly asks this question:
Is it because we Canadians are eight times more criminally minded than others? Is it because we have too many bad laws? Is it because we are puritanically punitive? Is it because Canadian authorities have a passion for putting people in prison?
I believe an outsider interested in the science of criminology would come to the inevitable conclusion that Canada is sending far too many people to prison.
A few days ago, during some discussion in this House, there was reference made to the fact that slums breed crime. This is so but it is also a fact statistically-and this can be confirmed not only in Canada but in the United Kingdom, and certainly in the United States-that in times of wealth, of prosperity, of buoyant economy, these are the times when there is an upsurge in crime.
All we have to do to see this, is regard the population problem with which we are faced right now in the educational field. We have discussed it in this Chamber from time to time. It is a crisis which is facing the universities. We are more concerned with the fact that there are a large number of Canadians in the teen age group who will likely be coming under our responsibility as criminal offenders because already they have established a pattern with respect to juvenile delinquency. Therefore I believe that this
May 17. 1965

two-pronged approach by the Government is a good one.
There is the approach by the experts who are going to look at the remission service scientifically, and they are going to have a lot to examine. It seems ridiculous to me that in the parole system of Canada we have only 29 parole officers for the whole Dominion of Canada.
Like some of my hon. friends who have already made contributions to this debate. I have visited several penal institutions. I think I have been in eight of our federal institutions, and I have been in some of them as many as six times. I have seen some wonderful things happen with people from these institutions. I remember well, as a trustee at Queen's University, watching a young man come up and receive his degree after he had served many years in the federal institution. That was some years ago, and I know what that man has done with his life since, and the impact that he had in university during his one year residency. Most of his study was completed in the cells. I could tell you about nurses who have distinguished themselves. I could tell you of things that are perhaps too intimate to bring into this place, but I can certainly assure you there are things such as reformation and turning bitter waters into sweetness.
During the sad days of the Second World War, when Britain was harassed and under immense danger, Churchill said something which we cannot forget. Churchill has said many things, and of course sociology was never a field in which he showed a particular interest; but on the subject of the treatment of the malefactor he said this:
The mood and temper of the public in regard to the treatment of crime and criminals is one of the most unfailing tests of the civilization of any country. A calm, dispassionate recognition of the rights of the accused, and even of the convicted criminal, against the State; a constant heartsearching of all charged with the deed of punishment; tireless efforts toward the discovery of regeneration processes; unfailing faith that there is a treasure, if you can find it, in the heart of every man; these are the symbols which, in the treatment of crime and criminals, make and measure the stored-up strength of a nation, and are sign and proof of the living virtue in it.
Only a great Englishman with a faith in the importance of the dignity of each human being, particularly in the midst of war when his nation was faced with crisis, was capable of such an utterance.
Recently I had some conversation with an interesting psychiatrist who has been working in this field of criminology for some
Penitentiaries Committee years, Dr. R. D. Buckner, who worked at Guelph reformatory during the years 1955, 1956, 1957 and 1958. Dr. Buckner was interested in the use that can be made of electroencephalograms. He takes the view, from his experiments with something like 300 inmates, that there is a clear relationship between crime and physiological damage to the brain. Out of 300 prisoners he examined there were 100 who showed some epileptic activity, and another 100 who showed through encephalography some evidence of theta waves, which to the professional is an indication of psychotic personality, of the psychopath, the person who habitually lies, who cannot be governed by cause and effect, who is egocentric and grandiloquent in his views and so on. His conclusions were that two out of three people who were in this Ontario institution showed physiologically some mental disposition to abnormality. The criminal person apparently springs from the maladjusted, the immature, and those of disordered character.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Recent studies in delinquency reveal that over 50 per cent of the subjects manifested serious signs of antisocial behaviour before the eighth year and another 40 per cent before the eleventh year. Nine out of ten delinquents showed signs of trouble before puberty. To my friend from Royal (Mr. Fair-weather)-and he has been my friend ever since we were at Osgoode Hall-I will say only this, though I should like to speak at greater length about minimum security work camps: Perhaps we have something to learn from Russia. It is conceivable that they are doing things in certain areas of penology which are more advanced than what we do in Canada. I think it is an interesting fact that in some camps they have in the North there is only one guard for 150 prisoners, and the guards are usually unarmed. I am not suggesting that large numbers of the people we have in our maximum security prisons could be taken for work in camps of this kind, but having visited St. Vincent de Paul, Kingston, Collins Bay, Joyceville and other institutions of this character, I honestly believe it is important that we should take many volunteer prisoners and give them a chance to work.
I have read the Glassco report and have some idea as to the contents of the Stevenson and Kellogg report. Generally speaking capital and labour in Canada are not very anxious that there should be any useful em-
1388	COMMONS
Penitentiaries Committee ployment provided within our penal system. They regard it as a threat. Why should they be asked to pay taxes to set up some kind of penal enterprise to compete against them?
I think it is of the essence that we should discover right now more fruitful ways of employing prisoners in our federal institutions.
I have seen a situation where a brick wall has gone up so many feet before being knocked down so that the work of building might be started once more. This is not good enough, because in the workshops of our institutions we have many skills. These skills should be put to use and I believe the time will come when we shall pay our prisoners reasonable sums with which they can assist their families. This is not unrealistic, it is not stupid; it is good logic and good business. It costs Canada something in the order of $250 a year to parole a man. Why should we keep a prisoner at a maximum or medium security institution at a cost in excess of $2,750 and allow him to remain idle so that there is an 80 per cent chance or better that he will commit further offences and return to confinement? In effect, why should we run schools for crime on a vast scale?
Some people are doing things of great value to effect rehabilitation and reform. One man who has impressed me very much is the chaplain at Kingston penitentiary, Rev. John A. Nickels. There are many men like him across this country. 1 think it is ridiculous what we pay these people. I discover that a chaplain serving in a federal penitentiary full time is paid $5,400. Can you imagine a man with an arts degree and a professional degree in theology, a married man with a family, providing for his family and paying for a home on a salary of $5,400 a year? On a part time basis the salary is $3,400. The chaplains interested in correctional work, both Roman Catholic and Protestant, are willing to take and train some of the best young men we have in Canada, and prepare them for this work.
A school like Queen's Theological College is prepared to gather together people of all faiths who are interested in this field. Very useful work is being done in Kingston under the leadership of William Lederman, dean of law at Queens' University, involving not only this school but the faculty of medicine, the department of psychology and Queen's Theological College. Penology seminars should be encouraged by the federal authorities and they should not be dictated to by the penal service. A lot of able professional people are interested today in these problems.

DEBATES	May 17. 1965
I am startled by the illogical way in which
the Federal Government is contributing to no less than 40 after-care agencies. What is the role of the after-care agency? The Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) has addressed himself to this problem. There has to be some clarification of function and financial support. I should like to see far more involvement on the part of the community as a whole. When a man gets into trouble in jail- and I know something about this because I am an experienced enough lawyer that a number of my clients have gone into jail; I have followed many of their careers and watched events in their families. After-care agencies, given the proper assistance, could very easily move in to help a man's family. I should like to see the churches brought into this picture to a greater degree. This might prevent the wife breaking up the home and moving in to live with someone else by whom she might have two or three other children.
It is a simple matter. The earliest question asked of man to God was: Am I my brother's keeper? We may deny our responsibility in other directions, but in this we cannot, because these people in the cells are in our power; we are their keeper. We are not doing a very good job. I believe that under the present Minister of Justice who has already analysed this subject to my satisfaction in a scholarly, sober and thorough way, the situation is bound to improve. I think it is time Parliament and the country as a whole took a close look at it.
Recently in Kingston Penitentiary there was a visit by Dr. Ernest Gordon. Some hon. Members will probably remember him. He wrote a book called the Valley of the Kwai. He commanded one of the Highland Regiments and was in captivity by the Japanese for a long time. He has been dean of Princeton Theological College. Recently he visited Kingston Penitentiary for several days. There used to be a situation at Kingston that even during church services there was a machine gun behind the pulpit ready to fire through a tiny hole. But that is not the case any more. There is a new atmosphere. Today in Kingston chapel no person is armed and there is practically no appearance of guards. Inmates who go there do so on a voluntary basis. This has had an electrifying effect. It takes some courage for some of these people who have a reputation for toughness to leave their cells to attend regular worship. I think the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) was present at Easter when the place was
May 17, 1965

packed. This is something completely contrary to anything experienced in the penitentiary before.
How did this come about? It came about because of the courage and leadership of the man Nickels who was naval padre on one of the ships of the Member for-

Certain proposals have been made recently by the hon. Member for Greenwood. They were sensible suggestions. I think, frankly, his bill on the Durham rule which I helped to talk out-

I did what I felt was correct at the time. But I have gone back through his speech and read a great deal more about the Durham rule, and it seems to me some of those suggestions are the kind we must bear in mind when we examine the penitentiaries.
Perhaps I have burdened the House for too long. I should like to conclude by reading part of a letter I received as a result of one of my visits to Kingston penitentiary. Incidentally, a number of Members from all parties have been active in these penitentiaries. I am in Kingston very often and I know that the presence of a Member of Parliament in these institutions is of considerable psychological importance. May I read extracts from this letter?
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Sir, you and your son were guests at our chapel in Kingston penitentiary and I was one of the inmates who listened as you read the Bible lesson and, afterward, spoke on the frailty and doubt that assails men who represent other men in Government. As I listened something happened inside me; it was like a rent in the fabric of a dam, as though all my life I had been listening for some sign that there was indeed flesh and blood and benevolent intelligence somewhere. Here was a confirmation of a hope which had almost ceased to exist. From my position in the pecking order, it is so easy to believe that the people of government, somehow, get there by being visitors from an enemy planet. I felt within me, as I listened, a burst of emotion, a crying, that came not only from recognition of humanity in a fellowman, but from a deep relief that I was still able to recognize, and feel emotion for, something worthy. Over the years of my life, I have managed, in self-defence or survival, to grow a hard crust over the emotional part of me. Perhaps I raised my own self-image by deriding and trampling better men. You touched me deeply
Penitentiaries Committee and I'm grateful. I think from now on I'll listen a little more carefully for the voices motivated by high principles rather than the voices of the cynics. Just so you will know this letter is without ulterior motivation I shall refrain from adding my signature.
That day I had my son, 17 years old, with me. He spent quite a bit of time with a woman who was perhaps my age, or maybe a little older, in the women's penitentiary, where we had doughnuts and coffee after their service.
I asked my son what this woman was interested in and what they were talking about. He said she was terribly concerned about how he was getting along with the new mathematics course and she wanted to know how he was coping with the problems of French, Latin, and so on. Of course she would be interested in these things; she had five children, she was a human being, and she had committed one crime in her life-she had killed somebody. I mention that-

I hear a bit of laughter over there, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to point out that we have to approach crime and the crime prone with a little humanity. The other day I was travelling in the train and met a recent graduate from the University of Saskatchewan, Stanley Nottingham, of Saskatoon -and this is something the hon. Member for Saskatoon (Mrs. Jones) will know-who told me that Leo Ouellette of Saskatoon was a troublemaker of long criminal record. He was a son of good parents who had always lived in dignity within the law. Ouellette was shot in a tavern. The autopsy revealed that he suffered subdural haematoma, which I am told is a severe bruise on the brain, of long standing. I believe that Dr. Lewis Brand of Saskatoon, who is well known to the Conservative ranks, was familiar with the details.
I am not advocating any policy of softness, but I do believe that when Members of this House of Commons go into jails it will be their moral duty to visit these places, not with any softness or sentiment, fully recognizing the danger that accompanies our police officers, but believing that reform is possible. We must be imaginative to fight crime, crime that is more ugly and more dangerous to our society today than perhaps at any time in the past. We must recognize that our purpose is not to be vengeful, but rather to deter crime and, above all, to reform.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that my recommendation with respect to work camps in

Penitentiaries Committee the North brings laughter. I would like to suggest that the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) take a very close look at the penitentiary service and make some kind of assessment as to what type of good mechanical, electrical or other work could be done in those institutions which would not seriously imperil labour or industry in Canada which now feels so sensitive that they would be adversely affected. I believe we should approach this problem from that point of view and permit people to work far harder and longer hours, and be paid. That is something that I think will ultimately come about.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to be the desire of all hon. Members of the House to proceed to the establishment of the committee as quickly as possible. Therefore I am not going to take many minutes in presenting a few ideas in this respect; in fact, I am going to restrict my remarks to making one major point as we proceed to set up this important Committee. The great concern, as I listened to other Members, seemed to me that this might be just another device brought forward by the Government as a delaying procedure.
It is some 30 years since the Parliament of Canada began to take a serious interest in the problem of penal reform and bringing our system of penology into line with the modern concepts of rehabilitation and welfare. Several hon. Members, including the hon. Member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) have referred to the two major studies that were made in this connection, the first being the Archambault Report, and later the Fauteux Report. Someone has said that it requires a minimum of 30 years between the time an idea is germinated and the occasion when it is implemented in the form of legislation. If this is true in reference to the subject of penal reform, Mr. Speaker, we are due for very drastic action in this field by 1968 at the latest. According to the progress that has been made in the intervening years, we are going to have to move very quickly indeed. Others have made some reference to the excellent work that was done by Hon. Davie Fulton when he was Minister of Justice. He moved into the field of establishing a more suitable facility which would fit into the modern concepts of penology, and we are all familiar with the minimum security institutions that were established under his direction.
Mr. Speaker, the point I want to deal with tonight is the fear that the present adminis-

DEBATES	May 17, 1985
tration is going to move toward the construction of maximum security institutions before this committee even has a chance to meet and consider the broad aspects of modem penology. I get this impression, for example from the statement that was made when the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) visited St. Vincent de Paul Penitentiary last October. On that occasion it was not a quiet or an unreported visit. Many hon. Members who have spoken in this discussion thus far have talked about their own experience in visiting penal institutions, and most of those visits have been carried out without the limelight of publicity. Last October the Minister of Justice took a group of some 100 reporters along to St. Vincent de Paul Penitentiary, and they were so shocked at what they saw, and the Minister was so shocked that he said, "There must be a quick end to what I call detestable conditions". It was shortly after that the announcement was made by the Government concerning the construction of new institutions, not of the minimum security variety but of the maximum security variety. I am hoping that these words of the Minister are not merely for the sake of effect; that it is not just a propaganda effort to lull those such as the Canadian Corrections Association, the John Howard Society and all the other voluntary groups that have been working in this field into thinking that something concrete will be done in this important area.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I am hoping that before we make any wrong moves in regard to dealing with the provision of extended institutional and custodial care, the committee about to be set up will have an opportunity to take a very careful look at the modern principles of penology as they have been clearly enunciated in this House and outside this House on many occasions. There is a need for a statement on principles and policies in the federal correctional field; and, more important, there is need for positive action based on those principles.
The principles which have motivated our attitude to the care and handling of criminals have been enunciated already this evening in this House. There is the revenge or punitive approach, the deterrent approach; and there is the conversion and rehabilitation approach. I think there is no one in this House-there has not been in this discussion up to the present moment-who would support the punitive or deterrent principle. Obviously the pendulum has swung in the direction of conversion and rehabilitation. This is for obvious reasons,
May 17, 1965

when you consider that under the present system, which has been largely deterrent and punitive, the recidivist rate in Canada is some 85 per cent of the prison population. As the Commission for Penitentiaries announced, I believe in the report of the Department of Justice for the year 1962-63, the prison population is growing rapidly, particularly in the under 21 age category. So I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker, this is dramatic evidence that the program exercised thus far has been less than successful.
In stressing the reform and the rehabilitation approach I should like to suggest that rather than thinking of custodial care and of increasing custodial facilities to deal with crime we should be thinking in terms of reform within society. This approach covers the whole gamut of social welfare problems at the present time.
I am not going to go into detail as to why crime is increasing, why mental illness is increasing or why drug addiction is on the increase. These are by products of an age of social change and social confusion. Certainly we are not going to resolve the problem by using the primitive method of shutting the offenders away from society for a shorter or longer period and hoping that automatically they will return to that society able to cope adequately, when before they were quite incapable of dealing with the situation.
This is why I quarrel with my hon. friend for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) in his rather contradictory presentation here tonight. I quarrel with him on two points. First of all, he regards the area north of the 60th parallel- and this unfortunately has been an attitude which has permeated the whole administration-as an area suitable for only the antisocial elements of Canadian society. Then in his observation a few moments ago the hon. Member for Leeds contradicted himself by saying that if we are going to reform offenders within society they must have access to community facilities, they must have access to community services, that there must be the atmosphere within the community itself which helps to carry out the rehabilitation process. I am sure that the isolation of the North would not be a conducive atmosphere in this regard.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the most useful method or technique of handling the problem is through the expansion of the probation and parole system. We have set up a parole board and a probation board, but we have not begun to tackle the aspect of this
Penitentiaries Committee problem which is the basic one, if the probation and parole boards are going to be able successfully to implement their programs and policies. We do not have the social workers trained in modern penology. We do not have the people capable of supervising the offenders when they are placed either on parole or on probation. I feel that before the Government moves to Em expensive program of constructing maximum security institutions they should give immediate attention to the social aspects of the problem; that is, making it possible for the offender to be rehabilitated and reformed within the community itself.
I do not want it to be understood, Mr. Speaker, that I am of the permissive school of thought so far as dealing with crime or with offences of any kind is concerned. I know in the family circle today that perhaps one of the reasons for the increase in juvenile deliquency is too much permissiveness on the part of parents who are afraid to administer the necessary disipline. If offenders are basically people who have offended against the rules of society and are antisocial in this respect, then, of course, some sort of discipline is required.
I rather subscribe to the viewpoint that the discipline be exerted within the community itself. If there must be punishment, let that punishment be the close supervision of the antisocial offender which comes from an adequate probation and parole system. To punish and not to restore is the greatest of all offences of which you could conceive. It is completely negative. You go out of the same door you came in. If man takes upon himself God's right to punish, which is what we do in the rigidly punitive approach to the problem of crime, then he must take upon himself God's promise to restore. I feel-and this is the point I want to make in concluding my remarks-that this can be done only within the community itself. This has been demonstrated in other countries practising progressive penal systems, and is also demonstrated by the failures shown by the figures in Canada quoted here in this discussion this evening.

Mr. Speaker, we in this group find ourselves a great deal puzzled by this resolution, as well as by the speech of the Parliamentary Secretary in introducing the resolution. The Government of Canada has announced that it has appointed a Special Committee on Correctional Reform. In making the announce-

May 17. 1965
Penitentiaries Committee merit of the appointment of this committee on April 9, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) listed the terms of reference of the committee and I should like to read a few of them:
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
"To study the broad field of corrections, in its widest sense, from the initial investigation of an offence through to the final discharge of a prisoner from imprisonment or parole, including such steps and measures as arrest, summonsing, bail, representation in Court, conviction, probation, sentencing, training, medical and psychiatric attention, relief, parole, pardon-
And so on.
Having appointed a committee of experts to study the whole field and make recommendations, the implementation of which could change the entire prison population in terms of numbers, length of sentence and the kind of treatment they will receive, the Government at the same time has announced its intention to establish a parliamentary committee to consider prisons. How can such a committee make recommendations about prisons before knowing what the expert commission will recommend as to the kind of correctional system we ought to have? How could that committee make recommendations before it knew the objectives of the recommendations of that expert commission?
We are being asked by the Government to approve a program for building prisons and correctional institutions in Canada as outlined by the Parliamentary Secretary this evening. How ridiculous can the Government get? On the one hand it appoints a committee to look into the whole question of correctional institutions and, I hope, the broad question of expansion in the field of probation, which will in years to come result in a sharp decline in the prison population and a complete stoppage of the year by year increase, while at the same time it proposes a tremendous construction program.
I do not have before me the newspaper article, but in an issue of the Globe and Mail of a few weeks ago a judge estimated the program, to which the Government has committed itself, at a potential cost of $120 million over the next ten years. It seems completely idiotic that the Government should decide in advance to build $120 million or $100 million worth of new correctional institutions, at the same time it is asking a committee to look into the question of our correctional institutions, and to report as to whether we ought to have a different approach to this situation. I have asked on several occasions, specifically

tonight when I asked a question of the Parliamentary Secretary, about the specific program to build detention units to which the Government has committed itself. I understand these are to be maximum security prisons. The Parliamentary Secretary told us this evening that there are to be ten built across Canada.

speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I should like to state that I made no such statement. There is to be one built in each penitentiary district of which there are four.

speechtext:
I will accept the Parliamentary Secretary's statement, but there are plans to build a number of these institutions.
Dr. Jaffray, who died recently, wrote in an article which appeared in a correctional magazine that on the basis of the experience of countries like Great Britain, we were planning to build at least twice as many of these institutions as necessary. I understand that the liaison committee established by the Canadian Corrections Association and the John Howard Society of Canada has been meeting with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) and his department, and has had an opportunity of looking at the plans. Reports indicate that that committee was horrified by the plan which provided, among other things, for the construction of cells in which there is to be no light except that which comes from a skylight system. Reports indicate that the committee informed the Minister and his officials that they were very disturbed in this regard, but that their protests were ignored.
In the event that hon. Members think I am exaggerating, I have before me a telegram which was sent to the Minister of Justice by the Canadian Corrections Association signed by one of the people the Minister thinks is so expert he qualifies to act on the royal commission of experts. That man is Mr. William McGrath. I should like to read this telegram into the record. The Parliamentary Secretary was very careful not to put it on the record during his statement this evening. I believe it was sent to the Minister on May 7, although I will not vouch for that date. I am sure that the contents are correct.
The telegram states:
Having seen the plans of the new federal penitentiaries under consideration or proposed for the future the Canadian Corrections Association feels obliged to express its serious concern to the Minister of Justice.
These structures appear to have been developed without regard to the study program objectives
May 17, 1965

of the Penitentiary Service and we therefore request that the design for the maximum security institutions be placed before the proposed Parliamentary Committee for thorough examination and that no new units be contracted for or constructed until such examination has taken place.
Further, we request that the construction of the special detention unit in the Province of Quebec be stopped immediately and no further such units be contracted for or constructed until a thorough examination of the plans be made by the proposed Parliamentary Committee.
These special detention units are completely unacceptable to the Canadian Corrections Association on the basis of scientific evidence related to the effects of psychological and physical isolation. Among other things we fear the deterioration of inmates who are confined in cells without windows.
Mr. McGrath is the Executive Secretary of the Canadian Corrections Association.
It seems to me there is little purpose in appointing a parliamentary committee or a royal commission to study the whole question in all its facets at a time when the Government seems determined to go ahead with a program to build maximum security units which have been criticized and condemned
Business of the House
by the people who have given the most thought and the most study to the question of what is needed in the field of correction in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock.
